---
title: "Zero-metallicity gas: equation of state and opacity"
---

Everything in this book, the steady model and the TITAN runs, uses the same microphysics: an ideal gas of
hydrogen and helium in LTE ionization equilibrium, and continuum mean opacities computed from first principles.
The composition is $X = 0.76$, $Y = 0.24$, $Z = 0$, as in the MESA-QUEST inlist.

## Saha equilibrium {#sec-saha}

The species are H, H$^+$, He, He$^+$, He$^{2+}$ and e$^-$. With $\lambda_e^{-3} \equiv (2\pi m_e kT/h^2)^{3/2}$, the
Saha equations{{< src eos::saha >}} are

$$
\frac{n_{\rm H^+}n_e}{n_{\rm H^0}} = \lambda_e^{-3}e^{-\chi_{\rm H}/kT},\qquad
\frac{n_{\rm He^+}n_e}{n_{\rm He^0}} = 4\lambda_e^{-3}e^{-\chi_{\rm He\,I}/kT},\qquad
\frac{n_{\rm He^{2+}}n_e}{n_{\rm He^+}} = \lambda_e^{-3}e^{-\chi_{\rm He\,II}/kT},
$$ {#eq-saha}

closed by charge neutrality, which is solved for $n_e$. The pressure is that of the particles plus blackbody
radiation,

$$
P = (n_{\rm H} + n_{\rm He} + n_e)\,kT + \tfrac13 aT^4 ,
$$ {#eq-pressure}

and the specific entropy is the Sackur–Tetrode sum over species plus radiation,

$$
s = \frac{k}{\rho}\sum_i n_i\left[\frac52 + \ln\!\left(\frac{g_i}{n_i}\Big(\frac{2\pi m_i kT}{h^2}\Big)^{3/2}\right)\right]
+ \frac{4aT^3}{3\rho} .
$$ {#eq-entropy}

The browser core reproduces the Julia implementation to $10^{-9}$ in $n_e$ and the ionized fraction
{{< test saha_matches_reference "Saha vs Julia" >}}, and in $P$, $e$ and $s$
{{< test eos_matches_reference "EOS vs Julia" >}}.

## Thermodynamic derivatives {#sec-thermo}

Convection and sound waves need derivatives of $P$ and $s$. With
$\chi_\rho = \partial\ln P/\partial\ln\rho|_T$, $\chi_T = \partial\ln P/\partial\ln T|_\rho$,
$s_\rho = \partial s/\partial\ln\rho|_T$ and $s_T = \partial s/\partial\ln T|_\rho$:

$$
\nabla_{\rm ad} = \Big(\chi_T - \chi_\rho\frac{s_T}{s_\rho}\Big)^{-1},\quad
\Gamma_1 = \chi_\rho - \chi_T\frac{s_\rho}{s_T},\quad
\delta = \frac{\chi_T}{\chi_\rho},\quad
c_P = s_T - s_\rho\,\delta .
$$ {#eq-thermo}

These are evaluated{{< src eos::eos_state >}} in $(\ln\rho, \ln T)$, which stays well conditioned when
$\beta \ll 1$. The Julia code uses exact forward-mode automatic differentiation through the Saha solve, so its
derivatives can enter a Newton–Raphson Jacobian (@sec-titan-port). Three checks pin them:

- the fully ionized gas plus radiation has $\Gamma_1(\beta) = (32 - 24\beta - 3\beta^2)/(24 - 21\beta)$, reproduced to $10^{-5}$ at $\beta = 0.5$, 0.1 and 0.01
  {{< test gamma1_fully_ionized_radiation "Γ₁(β)" >}};
- $\nabla_{\rm ad}$ tends to 0.4 for a neutral gas and to 0.25 when radiation dominates {{< test nabla_ad_limits "∇ad limits" >}};
- the browser core agrees with the Julia derivatives to $10^{-6}$ {{< test eos_matches_reference "derivatives vs Julia" >}}.

In the hydrogen ionization zone the gas is soft: at $P_{\rm gas} \approx 30$ dyn cm$^{-2}$, $\Gamma_1$ drops to about
0.97 near 8000 K **[computed]**.

## Mean opacities {#sec-opacity}

The Rosseland and Planck means are

$$
\frac{1}{\kappa_R} = \frac{\int(\kappa_\nu^{\rm abs}+\kappa_\nu^{\rm sc})^{-1}\,\partial_TB_\nu\,d\nu}{\int\partial_TB_\nu\,d\nu},\qquad
\kappa_P = \frac{\int\kappa_\nu^{\rm abs}B_\nu\,d\nu}{\int B_\nu\,d\nu} ,
$$ {#eq-rosseland}

on 4000 frequencies, with every absorption edge placed on the frequency grid. The continuum sources are:

- Thomson and H Rayleigh scattering;
- hydrogenic bound-free from H I ($n\le12$) and He II ($n\le8$), with LTE level populations and Kramers cross sections $\sigma_n = 2.815\times10^{29}Z^4/(n^5\nu^3)$;
- He I ground-state bound-free;
- free-free on H$^+$, He$^+$ and He$^{2+}$ (Gaunt factor 1);
- H$^-$ bound-free and free-free [@john1988].

Stimulated emission is included. **No bound–bound lines and no molecules are included.** $\kappa_R$ is therefore a
lower bound near $10^4$–$10^5$ K, where line opacity in OPAL-type tables can raise it by a factor of a few, and
below about 2500 K, where H$_2$ collision-induced absorption would matter.

The means are tabulated on $\log T = 3.3$–8.0 (step 0.005) and $\log R = -12$–1 (step 0.025), with
$R = \rho/T_6^3$, and interpolated with C¹ bicubic (Catmull–Rom) weights{{< src opacity::KapTable::kappa_r >}}. The
browser uses the same table, stored in single precision, and agrees with the Julia interpolation to $10^{-5}$
{{< test kappa_matches_reference "κ vs Julia" >}}. At high temperature $\kappa_R$ tends to the electron-scattering
value 0.350 cm² g⁻¹ {{< test kappa_high_t_limit "Thomson limit" >}}. (The usual $0.2(1+X) = 0.352$ uses $m_p$ in
place of $m_{\rm H}$.) For the TITAN infall runs the table was extended to $\log T = 3.0$ and $\log R = -20$, with
identical values on the original nodes **[computed]**.

## The opacity cliff {#sec-cliff}

At zero metallicity there are no metals to supply free electrons once hydrogen recombines. Between about 8000 and
6000 K the Rosseland mean therefore falls by orders of magnitude, from the electron-scattering value to the small
H$^-$ opacity. We call this the *opacity cliff*. It matters twice in this book. It is why the infall photosphere sits
near 6000–7500 K on both branches of steady solutions (@sec-observer). And it is why the extended atmosphere
of the steady model drains in TITAN (@sec-hydrostatic-surface).

Move the density and watch the ionization fractions and the two means. The ionization edge moves to lower
temperature at lower density (Saha), and the Rosseland mean collapses with the hydrogen ionized fraction. The
Planck mean (absorption only) falls far below the Rosseland mean wherever scattering dominates. The panels show
$\nabla_{\rm ad}$ and $\Gamma_1$ at the same density: both dip in the ionization zones.
